Schema-constrained decoding (the strict structured-output modes some providers offer) restricts which token sequences can be produced, so the result parses and has the declared types and enum values. Plain JSON mode promises only syntactically valid JSON, and ordinary function calling without a strict mode may not even guarantee the schema, so check which guarantee your provider documents.
Truncated output has no balanced end, so it is skipped rather than 'completed': guessing the missing tail can turn a cut-off reply into a plausible but wrong record.

Truncated output has no balanced end, so it is skipped rather than 'completed': guessing the missing tail can turn a cut-off reply into a plausible but wrong record. Caveat: scanning resumes after the skipped opener, so a complete inner object of a truncated outer value (for example '{"a": {"b": 1}') is still returned as a candidate; the schema's required keys usually reject it, and a reply that ended mid-value should be treated as suspect.
